geometry.rationale: Figure 1 better preserves the intended unit-circle construction with a fixed circular geometry, two radii to P and Q, shaded angular sector, inner angle arcs, point labels, axes with arrowheads, and the bottom explanatory caption in proportions closer to the textbook layout. Figure 2 has the same basic elements, but its plot-frame mapping can non-uniformly scale the circle into an ellipse, its circle is split into solid and dashed arcs that do not clearly match the full unit-circle outline, and its overall layout/label proportions are more generic and less faithful.

interactivity.rationale: Figure 1's controls correctly recompute and redraw the moving point P, fixed point Q, radii, labels, shaded sector, and readout over essentially the full unit-circle angle range, and its animation demonstrates approach from both sides. Figure 2's sliders do update the basic geometry, but they are narrowed to only 0.05–1.5 radians, so the target angle cannot be relocated around the unit circle; its left/right animations also degenerate at the slider endpoints because clamping can make x equal c immediately, causing the advertised approach-from-one-side animation to do nothing or nearly nothing.

faithfulness.rationale: Figure 1 is much more visually faithful: it preserves the main composition with labeled points P and Q, the red and black radius segments, shaded sector, angle labels, arrow, axes, blue circle, and the explanatory caption. Figure 2 has the general geometry but loses the important P/Q coordinate labels, shows stray punctuation instead, has a broken/obscured caption, and its layout feels less like the original despite capturing the sector and circle.

labels.rationale: Figure 1 includes the main textbook labels for P(cos x, sin x), Q(cos c, sin c), the angle labels x and c, and the full explanatory caption in a readable box, with generally clear placement. Figure 2 omits the key P and Q coordinate labels, has stray/partial markings near the arc, and its bottom caption is severely clipped and incomplete, making the labeling much less faithful and readable.

concept.rationale: Figure 1 more accurately represents the brief's general unit-circle argument: it draws the full unit circle, lets both angles range essentially over 0 to 2π, and correctly labels P(cos x, sin x) and Q(cos c, sin c), matching the arbitrary-angle continuity motivation (L00007-L00013, L00016). Figure 2 correctly places P and Q for its restricted first-quadrant range, but it draws only a partial/missing unit circle and limits x and c to about 0.05–1.5 radians, which makes the visual argument look much less general than the stated continuity at every point c; this weakens the concept compared with Figure 1 (L00013, L00016).

aggregator.explanation: Figure 1 is stronger across all dimensions: it preserves the intended unit-circle construction with a fixed circular outline, radii to P and Q, shaded sector, angle labels, readable coordinate labels, and the explanatory caption, while Figure 2 omits or clips key labels and caption content. Figure 1 also supports the intended generality and interactions over essentially the full angle range, whereas Figure 2 restricts the angles to a narrow first-quadrant interval, can distort or partially render the circle, and has endpoint issues in its approach animations.

geometry.rationale: Figure 1 much more accurately reconstructs the textbook structure because it shows both panels (a) and (b) simultaneously with separate axis ranges, tick labels, panel labels, vector-field grids, red oriented curves, and the correct vertical segment/parabolic arc layout. Figure 2 collapses the two-panel figure into one switchable plot with a single shared domain, adds extra ticks and Bézier control handles/dashed control polygon, and therefore loses the original side-by-side/stacked panel topology and proportions even though the individual paths and vector field are recognizable.

interactivity.rationale: Figure 2’s controls more directly and correctly update the advertised quantities: the path buttons reset the selected path, dragging control points recomputes and redraws the curve, moving-point overlay, dot product, and total line integral, and the t slider updates the local field/tangent display. Figure 1’s dragging and t slider generally work, but it does not provide a clearly updated total line-integral readout—only a partial integral to the current t in the local card—and its panel toggle merely changes the active overlay while both panels remain drawn, making the interaction less faithful and less complete.

faithfulness.rationale: Figure 1 is much more recognizable as the textbook figure because it preserves the two stacked panels, pale green vector-field backgrounds, black axes with italic labels, red curve/segment paths, panel labels, and the overall composition. Figure 2 only shows a single interactive panel with mismatched scale/extent, added colored control-point markers and diagnostic arrows/text, and it loses the original two-panel textbook layout, making it look more like a custom demo than the source figure.

labels.rationale: Figure 1 has far better label quality because it includes the main textbook annotations for both panels: the title, x and y axis labels, tick labels including −π/2, curve label C, and panel labels (a) and (b). Figure 2 only shows a single enlarged panel, omits the second panel and its labels entirely, lacks the panel labels, introduces many non-original interface annotations and extra numerical labels, and its diagram labels do not match the original as closely.

concept.rationale: Figure 1 more accurately teaches the intended geometry because it shows both labeled panels at once with the same field F=(cos x, sin x), the vertical segment at x=−π/2 directed from y=2 to y=1, and an exact y=x² parabolic arc from (−1,1) to (2,4) whose orientation first goes downward and then upward/right (L00007-L00039, L00042). Figure 2’s field and individual default paths are mostly correct, but it collapses the two-panel comparison into a single switchable plot and frames the given paths as draggable Bézier control-point curves, which weakens and can alter the fixed textbook distinction between the two integration paths and their differently scaled panels (L00042).

aggregator.explanation: Figure 1 is the clear overall winner because it preserves the original two-panel textbook structure, labels, axis ranges, vector fields, red paths, and intended geometric distinction between the vertical segment and parabolic arc, whereas Figure 2 collapses the comparison into a single switchable plot with mismatched scale and extra non-original annotations. Figure 2 has stronger interactive behavior, especially for draggable paths and updated integral readouts, but that advantage is outweighed by its weaker visual faithfulness, missing panel labels, altered composition, and Bézier-control framing that makes the fixed textbook paths less faithful than Figure 1.

geometry.rationale: Figure 1 much more accurately reconstructs the textbook PEM fuel-cell schematic: it preserves the large grey end plates, black gas-flow channels, central anode/membrane/cathode proportions, external wire with a prominent yellow zigzag load, labeled inlet/outlet arrows, molecule/charge counts, and bottom pointer labels in the expected layout. Figure 2 captures the general concept but is more schematic and simplified, with compressed proportions, altered manifold geometry, a much less faithful external load/circuit, fewer static particles and reaction-site details, and labels/arrows placed in a layout that departs noticeably from the original.

interactivity.rationale: Figure 2’s step controls and continuous animation actually move H2, H+, electrons, O2, and water along the intended paths, so the advertised fuel-cell cycle is recomputed and redrawn much more faithfully; Figure 1 mostly pulses opacity on static particles/arrows and uses step buttons for narration/highlights rather than showing the splitting and transport process. Figure 2’s feed-rate slider redraws arrows including heads and changes animation speed, whereas Figure 1 changes only line strokes while leaving arrowheads inconsistent and even at a zero feed rate still shows nonzero current/flow thickness. Both label/clean-flow toggles work, but Figure 2’s interactions are overall more correct despite its narrower slider range and step navigation limits.

faithfulness.rationale: Figure 1 is much more visually faithful to the textbook figure: it preserves the central purple anode/cathode and blue membrane, the yellow electric-power element, labeled gas and water flows, charge icons, arrows, and molecule placement in a composition very close to the original. Figure 2 retains the broad fuel-cell layout but is overly simplified, uses a different muted color scheme, omits most molecule and charge details, and changes the electric-power symbol and overall visual density enough that it resembles a schematic abstraction rather than the original figure.

labels.rationale: Figure 1 has all the required textbook labels with correct wording and generally readable sizing and placement, including clear bottom labels for Anode, Proton exchange membrane, and Cathode. Figure 2 also includes the main labels, but several are noticeably smaller, the bottom membrane/electrode labels are cramped and less readable at inline size, and the overall annotation quality is less faithful to the original.

concept.rationale: Figure 1 more faithfully represents the required fuel-cell concepts: hydrogen enters the anode side, electrons go through the external load labeled Electric power, protons pass through the proton exchange membrane, oxygen enters the cathode side, water exits lower right, and unused hydrogen exits lower left, matching the spatially separated half-reactions in the brief (L00014, L00017). Figure 2 is broadly correct in layout, but its stepped cathode reaction depicts only two protons and two electrons combining with one O2 molecule to produce two water molecules, which is chemically inconsistent with the brief’s statement that each oxygen atom takes two protons to form water and with the overall cathode combination of oxygen, protons, and electrons (L00014-L00017).

aggregator.explanation: Figure 1 is clearly stronger overall because it much more faithfully matches the textbook PEM fuel-cell schematic in geometry, visual density, labels, color structure, molecule/charge placement, and the key conceptual pathways for hydrogen, protons, electrons, oxygen, water, and unused hydrogen. Figure 2 has better dynamic interactivity, with particles and flows actually moving through the cycle, but it is more simplified visually, less faithful in its circuit/load and annotation layout, and includes a chemically inconsistent cathode-reaction depiction relative to the brief.

geometry.rationale: Figure 2 better preserves the likely textbook geometry by laying out panels (a) through (d) simultaneously with the correct counts of axial/equatorial sites, fluorine bonds, and lone-pair rays for each arrangement. Figure 1 has a more polished trigonal-bipyramidal shell and cleaner leader construction, but geometrically it only shows panel (a) plus one selected arrangement at a time in the main view, hiding the other comparison structures and therefore losing the original multi-panel spatial layout and element count.

interactivity.rationale: Figure 1 more correctly implements the requested interactions: clicking the actual Axial/Equatorial HTML labels changes the highlighted family and the arrangement selector/step buttons switch the active (b), (c), and (d) molecule with labels and narration kept in sync. Figure 2’s highlight buttons and hitboxes mostly work, but its panel controls only dim nonselected panels rather than really toggling/cycling between (b), (c), and (d), so the advertised comparison state is less clearly changed; Figure 1’s main flaw is that some registered leader-line click targets only show a popup instead of highlighting, but the actual requested labels still work.

faithfulness.rationale: Figure 2 is more recognizable as the original because it presents all four labeled arrangements (a–d) in a horizontal sequence with green octahedral frameworks, red highlighted bonds, and F/Cl labels, matching the textbook figure’s overall composition. Figure 1 renders the individual structures larger, but it only shows the reference and one comparison panel in the screenshot, omits much of the multi-panel layout, and its labels/spacing make it look less like the original figure at a glance.

labels.rationale: Figure 2 has the better label coverage because it includes all four subfigure labels (a)–(d) and the relevant F/Cl annotations across the comparison, whereas Figure 1 only shows panels (a) and (b) and therefore omits many required labels from the original. Figure 1's few labels are larger and more readable, but it is much less complete and even has an inaccurate-looking bold '(B)' label, while Figure 2's labels are cramped and small but more closely match the full set of original annotations.

concept.rationale: Figure 1 more accurately represents the required concepts: it places panel (b)'s two lone pairs in equatorial sites to give the observed T-shaped ClF3, panel (c)'s lone pairs one axial/one equatorial, and panel (d)'s lone pairs both axial as the greatest lone-pair–bond-pair repulsion case, matching the authored brief and VSEPR explanation (L00010-L00012, L00021). Figure 2 gets the main arrangements mostly correct visually, but its panel (c) explanation falsely says the axial lone pair has 90° repulsion from three equatorial bonds even though panel (c) has one equatorial lone pair and only two equatorial F bonds, conflating lone-pair contacts with bond-pair contacts and mis-teaching the repulsion comparison (L00021). Figure 1 also more cleanly states the axial/equatorial distinction and equatorial preference from the 120° spacing, whereas Figure 2’s panel (a) gray center-to-site rays can misleadingly imply all five sites are bonds rather than just a trigonal-bipyramidal positional frame (L00007, L00010, L00021).

aggregator.explanation: Figure 2 is the stronger overall recreation because it preserves the full four-panel textbook layout with panels (a)–(d), more complete F/Cl and subfigure labeling, and the correct comparative geometry visible at once, whereas Figure 1 only shows the reference plus one selected arrangement and therefore loses much of the original composition and label set. Figure 1 has better authored interaction behavior and a cleaner conceptual explanation of the VSEPR repulsion ordering, but those strengths do not fully offset its missing multi-panel structure; Figure 2’s main relative weaknesses are less decisive controls and a misleading panel (c) explanation.

geometry.rationale: Figure 2 reconstructs the StyleGAN diagram geometry much more accurately: it includes the learned constant, three noise sheets, paired injection slabs, three style transforms, synthesis blocks with increasing spatial size, a separate final image plane, grouping braces, and routed arrows/bus lines with proportions and oblique depth closer to the textbook figure. Figure 1 captures the rough idea but uses cruder same-depth rectangular boxes, less accurate scaling and spacing, simpler line arrows, flat square noise sources instead of slanted sheets, and a less faithful output/image and block layout.

interactivity.rationale: Figure 2 has substantially more correct interactions: its trace control animates visible pulses from z to w, along the style bus to y1/y2/y3 and into the synthesis blocks, while also highlighting the relevant style/noise injection regions; its noise slider consistently updates displayed ψ, arrow thickness/opacity, noise slab opacity, and channel broadcast highlights. Figure 1 only steps through coarse highlights with status text rather than actually tracing the paths, and its ψ slider maps ψ=0 to a nonzero scale of 0.5, so the advertised noise magnitude cannot be turned off and the visual change is much less faithful.

faithfulness.rationale: Figure 2 is more recognizable as the original StyleGAN pipeline because it preserves the three labeled bands with curly braces, the top noise inputs, middle generative blocks, bottom style pathway, and repeated style/noise injections across the horizontal flow. Figure 1 has similar colored blocks but is more cramped and perspective-compressed, with the left grouping/braces and bottom style pathway less faithful and much of the labeling overlapping into an unreadable cluster.

labels.rationale: Figure 2 has more of the required labels visibly present, including the three style labels y1, y2, y3 and the noise labels, and its text is generally larger than Figure 1. Figure 1’s labels are often extremely small and crowded, especially in the lower style pathway where latent/intermediate variable and linear-transform labels overlap heavily and become hard to read. Figure 2 still has significant clutter and collisions around the left section labels and bottom annotations, but it preserves more readable and complete labeling overall.

concept.rationale: Figure 2 is conceptually stronger because it explicitly identifies the learned constant input in its interactive label, shows z mapping to w and then to three separate 2×1×512 linear transforms producing y₁–y₃, and depicts three noise maps with the correct 4×4×1/4×4×1/8×8×1 dimensions and broadcast-to-channels explanation (L00007). Figure 1 has many of the same labels, but the initial 4×4×512 block is not asserted to be a learned constant and the main synthesis/resolution progression is less clearly tied to the style/noise injections, so it teaches the architecture slightly less accurately (L00007). Both figures organize the branches more as horizontal bands with side braces rather than the brief’s three vertical columns with bottom underbrace labels, so neither is fully accurate on that organizational claim (L00007).

aggregator.explanation: Figure 2 is the clear overall winner because it more accurately reconstructs the StyleGAN architecture: it shows the learned constant, z-to-w mapping, three style transforms y1–y3, repeated noise inputs, synthesis blocks, routed buses, and grouping braces in a layout closer to the reference. Compared with Figure 2, Figure 1 is cruder and more cramped, with less faithful geometry, less readable labels, weaker depiction of style/noise injection, and interactions that only provide coarse highlights rather than visibly tracing the intended paths; its noise control also cannot truly reduce noise to zero.

geometry.rationale: Figure 1 more accurately reconstructs the textbook geometry: it builds a true 6×6×6 lattice with face gridlines, outer cube boundary, axis arrows, isometric camera, and method-specific highlighted slabs/strips/columns with plausible counts and spatial relationships for BatchNorm, GhostNorm, LayerNorm, GroupNorm, and InstanceNorm. Figure 2 has the same general cube idea but its opaque full-cell rendering obscures depth, lacks the outer/face grid and axis arrows, omits panel/title geometry cues, and uses less accurate highlighted extents for GhostNorm and GroupNorm, making the selected normalization scopes less faithful.

interactivity.rationale: Figure 1's controls consistently recompute the highlighted normalization scope, active button state, narration, μ/σ²/pooled-axis labels, and a method-dependent sweep that stays within the selected orange region. Figure 2's method buttons mostly recolor the correct cells, but its aggregation animation always advances by spatial-position slices regardless of the selected normalization type, so it does not correctly demonstrate pooling over batch or channel axes for BatchNorm, GhostNorm, LayerNorm, or GroupNorm; it also provides less updated explanatory state during the interaction.

faithfulness.rationale: Figure 1 is more visually faithful because it preserves the textbook-style light gray cube with orange highlighted normalization region, visible gridlines, axis labels, panel label “a)”, and the BatchNorm caption, making it immediately recognizable as the corresponding panel of the original. Figure 2 has the same basic cube-and-orange-slab idea, but its darker color scheme, missing panel letter/title near the cube, smaller labels, and less textbook-like presentation make it read less like the original figure at a glance.

labels.rationale: Figure 1 has more of the original labeling: it includes the panel marker "a)", the axis labels "Position", "Channel", and "batch index", and the large "BatchNorm" caption, whereas Figure 2 lacks the panel letter and the main bottom normalization label and has much smaller, less readable axis labels. Figure 1 is hurt by invented annotations such as "μ, σ²" and pooling notes plus some overlap/clutter near the bottom label, but Figure 2 omits more required original labels and relies mainly on UI text rather than diagram labels.

concept.rationale: Both figures correctly show BatchNorm as one channel pooled over batch and spatial position, LayerNorm as one batch instance pooled over channels and positions, GroupNorm as a per-sample subset of channels over positions, and InstanceNorm as one sample/channel over positions (L00007). Both figures, however, misrepresent GhostNorm relative to the brief: each shows a BatchNorm-like single-channel, subset-of-batch/all-position region, while the brief specifies all batch instances and all channels but not spatial position (L00007). Figure 1 is still slightly better because its μ/σ² marker and pooled-axis badges more explicitly teach which axes are aggregated for the four correctly implemented methods, whereas Figure 2 provides fewer in-scene conceptual annotations and makes the same GhostNorm error.

aggregator.explanation: Figure 1 is the clear overall winner: it more faithfully reconstructs the textbook-style cube with visible gridlines, axis arrows/labels, panel marker, BatchNorm caption, and method-specific highlighted regions, while Figure 2 is darker, less labeled, and its opaque cells obscure the geometry. Figure 1 also has stronger interactivity because its buttons update the highlighted scope, explanatory text, pooled-axis labels, and sweep animation consistently with the selected normalization method, whereas Figure 2’s animation incorrectly uses spatial slices for several methods. Both figures share a conceptual GhostNorm error, but Figure 1 better communicates the other normalization scopes and preserves more of the intended visual and labeling structure.

geometry.rationale: Figure 1 better preserves the seven-row decoder structure: each token row passes through embeddings, masked attention, residual additions, feed-forward/transform blocks, linear-softmax, and probability outputs, with many of the expected per-row nodes and arrows present. Figure 2 has cleaner proportions and styling, but it collapses much of the transformer internals into a single middle-row path, showing only one residual add per sublayer and one main flow arrow through the block, so it undercounts the row-wise topology of the original architecture.

interactivity.rationale: Figure 1’s K slider actually redraws the architecture with the selected number of transformer blocks and its trace animation follows the bottom “let” row through attention, residual additions, linear/softmax, and the “yourself” output, whereas Figure 2’s K slider only adds small layer indicator bars without recomputing or expanding the main decoder block. Figure 2 does implement persistent click highlighting better, but its large transformer hitbox likely covers the more specific residual/attention hitboxes and its trace is mostly a single bottom-row path rather than showing prefix aggregation through masked attention, while Figure 1’s main interaction shortcoming is the absence of persistent click highlighting despite otherwise functional tooltips/popups.

faithfulness.rationale: Figure 1 is more visually faithful because it preserves the full left-to-right composition of embeddings, masked transformer block, linear/softmax outputs, probability vectors, and the target-token labels on the far right. Figure 2 is recognizable but less faithful at a glance because several labels are clipped or missing, including the right-side target token labels and parts of headings/left words, making the original layout feel truncated.

labels.rationale: Figure 1 has smaller labels, but it preserves the key original annotations and token labels more completely, including the right-side target tokens. Figure 2’s labels are larger in places, but several are clipped or truncated, such as the top probability heading and the left token “courage,” and the important right-side target-token labels are missing or not visible, making it less faithful to the original.

concept.rationale: Figure 2 teaches the core concepts more correctly: it explicitly states that rows are computed side by side/in parallel while the lower-triangular causal mask prevents look-ahead, and it correctly shows shifted targets from <start>→It through let→yourself (L00007). Figure 1 gets the main token/target shift and causal mask mostly right, but its UI/popup language says the transformer layers process the states “sequentially,” which conflicts with the brief’s emphasis on parallel next-token prediction across positions, and its residual bypass drawing can misleadingly look like a top-row signal being broadcast to all positions rather than per-position residual connections (L00007).

aggregator.explanation: Figure 1 is stronger overall because it preserves the full decoder layout with per-token rows, embeddings, masked attention, residual/feed-forward structure, linear-softmax outputs, probability vectors, and visible target-token labels, while Figure 2 collapses much of the transformer internals and has clipped or missing labels. Figure 1 also has a more functional K slider and trace animation that redraws and follows the architecture more meaningfully, whereas Figure 2’s slider mostly adds layer indicators and its broad hitboxes/path obscure more specific behavior. Figure 2 is conceptually better at emphasizing parallel row computation and causal masking, but that advantage does not outweigh Figure 1’s clearer structural, visual, labeling, and interaction fidelity.

geometry.rationale: Figure 1 better preserves the likely textbook structure by showing both single-observer and two-observer constructions side by side, with the correct counts of observers, sightlines, angle arcs, h/t/d? labels, boat, shoreline, water boundary, and heavy black line-art styling. Figure 2 reduces the structure to one switchable scene at a time, adds non-original red/grey estimated/target boats and an in-canvas readout panel, uses different thin/dashed styling, and changes the relative shoreline/observer/boat layout enough that it is less faithful structurally.

interactivity.rationale: Figure 2's controls more directly recompute the geometry they advertise: the method radio buttons switch a single unified diagram and show only the relevant controls, the height and separation sliders redraw the observer geometry and estimated boat position, and degenerate triangulation cases such as parallel or behind-the-observer intersections are explicitly handled. Figure 1's height and separation sliders do trigger redraws, but the height and boat positions are clamped so the advertised distance change stalls at extremes, the triangulation is more of an arbitrary redrawing than a computed intersection, and its method toggle does not actually switch to a unified diagram or remove the inactive panel—it merely changes which panel title is emphasized while both panels remain visible.

faithfulness.rationale: Figure 1 is much more recognizable as the original because it preserves the two-panel composition, turquoise water/brown land/white sky color scheme, cliff-and-eye geometry, sightlines, sailboat, and labels for both the single-observer and triangulation setups. Figure 2 captures only a simplified single-observer schematic and replaces the original irregular coastline/cliff and detailed boat/observer styling with a blocky rectangular cliff and sparse elements, making it look less like the textbook figure at a glance.

labels.rationale: Figure 1 includes the key textbook labels across both original subfigures (h, α, d?, and the two-observer labels including β and t), whereas Figure 2 only represents the single-observer case and omits the second-panel annotations entirely. Figure 2's labels are more readable, but it adds many non-original UI/status labels and even an extra α near the boat, while Figure 1 better matches the original label set despite its labels being quite small.

concept.rationale: Figure 1 more faithfully represents the two intended geometric methods: its left panel shows a known observer height h above the water, a horizontal reference/horizon line, a downward sightline angle, and a horizontal d? distance to the boat, while its right panel shows two separated observers with baseline t whose rays intersect at the boat for triangulation, matching the brief (L00012, L00021-L00022). Figure 2’s single-observer construction is mostly correct, but its two-observer panel labels d? along a sight ray and reports an observer-to-boat Euclidean distance rather than the boat’s distance from the coast, which can teach the wrong quantity for the stated task (L00012, L00022); it also adds a true/estimated target setup whose “Target Boat Location” is not consistently the coast distance.

aggregator.explanation: Figure 1 is the stronger overall match because it preserves the original two-panel textbook structure, including both the single-observer height/angle/distance construction and the two-observer triangulation with the expected labels, sightlines, shoreline, boat, and visual styling. Figure 2 has more robust interactive controls and recomputes its displayed geometry more cleanly, but it departs more from the source figure by reducing or switching scenes, adding non-original target/estimate elements and status labels, and in the triangulation case conveying the wrong distance quantity relative to the coast.

geometry.rationale: Figure 2 better reconstructs the optical layout with a clearly convex objective, concave eyepiece, long f1 and shorter f2 spans in the correct Galilean afocal relationship, two parallel incoming rays that focus to the shared focal point and leave parallel, and the main structural labels/brackets/arcs placed with more faithful proportions. Figure 1 captures the same basic topology and even includes dashed continuations for both rays, but its overall proportions are more compressed, the eyepiece shape is less clear, the measurement/angle annotations are more schematic and less well integrated, and the ray/reference layout is less visually faithful to a textbook-style telescope diagram.

interactivity.rationale: Figure 2 has the more correct core interactions: dragging the d/angle marker recomputes the incoming angle and outgoing rays coherently, and dragging lens 2 updates the ray convergence/divergence with a live beam-state readout. Figure 1’s focal-length sliders and lens-2 drag mostly work, but its advertised input-angle handle is wired with the wrong sign, so the handle does not stay under the cursor and the angle change effectively runs backwards/jumps toward the clamp. Figure 2 is not perfect because its focal-length slider ranges and hard x-position clamp can prevent the afocal separation at some extremes, but Figure 1’s broken angle drag is a more direct failure of a requested control.

faithfulness.rationale: Figure 1 is more visually faithful overall: it preserves the thick upper purple ray, thinner lower ray, black input arrowheads, blue optical axis, lens labels, distance brackets, and the d/δo annotation in a composition that more closely resembles the reference. Figure 2 has a cleaner negative-lens shape, but it makes the rays more uniformly thin, replaces the prominent input arrowheads with small handle-like markers, and uses a different-looking δo angle annotation, so it reads less like the original at a glance.

labels.rationale: Figure 2 has the required optical labels more clearly and accurately placed overall: lens 1, lens 2, f1, f2, d, both δi labels, and δo are present, with δo placed beside the outgoing angle similarly to the reference. Figure 1 includes many of the same labels, but δo is tiny and cluttered near the dashed ray and d marker rather than clearly annotated on the right, and several diagram labels are harder to read due to smaller scale and crowding.

concept.rationale: Both figures correctly show the core afocal Galilean geometry at the default setting: a convex objective and concave eyepiece with parallel input rays focused to a shared off-axis point and re-emitted as a parallel bundle with larger angular deviation, consistent with the stated M = f1/f2 relation (L00007, L00010). Figure 1 is more conceptually careful when the eyepiece is moved out of the afocal condition, marking magnification as not applicable and hiding δₒ, while Figure 2 continues to display the assertion “δo/δi = f1/f2” even when its own beam readout says the exit beam is converging or diverging, which is misleading because δₒ as a single output-bundle angle and the telescope magnification relation apply to the afocal parallel-output case described in the brief (L00007, L00010).

aggregator.explanation: Figure 2 is stronger overall because it more accurately reconstructs the Galilean optical geometry and has clearer, better-placed labels such as f1, f2, d, δi, and δo, whereas Figure 1 is more compressed, more cluttered, and has a less clear concave eyepiece and angle/distance annotations. Figure 2 also handles the main drag interactions more coherently, while Figure 1’s input-angle handle is directly miswired and behaves backwards. Figure 1 is more visually faithful to the rendered reference and is more careful about hiding δo when the system is non-afocal, but those advantages do not outweigh Figure 2’s stronger geometry, labeling, and interaction behavior.
